summary: This document defines a YANG data model to configure and manage Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD). The modules conform to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA).

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9127 defines a standard way for a management system to set up BFD and read back how it is doing. BFD is the protocol two routers use to notice quickly that the path between them has broken. Because a BFD session can run over several kinds of path, the model is split into one module for each kind, all sharing the same definitions.

questions: what is the yang data model for bfd
what bfd path types does yang support
how is a bfd session identified in yang
subtitle: A set of YANG modules for configuring and monitoring BFD sessions on IP, MPLS and LAG paths.

tldr.problem: BFD detects liveness of many kinds of forwarding paths, but there was no standard data model to configure BFD or read its state, and no single key identifies a BFD session across path types.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a family of NMDA-conformant YANG modules: shared types, a common bfd container, and one module each for IP single-hop, IP multihop, LAG and MPLS LSPs.
tldr.outcome: Operators and tools get a common way to configure sessions, read per-session state and statistics, and receive notifications. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9314.

facts.label: Path types
facts.value: IP single-hop, IP multihop, MPLS LSP, LAG

today: RFC 9127 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9314. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document defines a YANG data model that can be used to configure and manage Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) of RFC 5880. BFD is a network protocol used for liveness detection of arbitrary paths between systems. The RFC lists the types of path over which BFD runs: two systems directly connected over IP, which is BFD over single-hop IP for IPv4 and IPv6 as in RFC 5881; two systems connected over multiple hops, as in RFC 5883; two systems connected over MPLS label switched paths, as in RFC 5884; and two systems connected over a Link Aggregation Group interface, as in RFC 7130. Two systems connected over pseudowires, which is Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification of RFC 5885, is not addressed by this document.

BFD typically does not operate on its own. Various control protocols, also known as BFD clients, use the services BFD provides for their own operation, as described in RFC 5882. The obvious candidates are the protocols that have no hellos of their own to detect failures, such as static routes, and the routing protocols whose hellos do not support sub-second failure detection, such as OSPF and IS-IS.

The YANG modules in this document conform to the Network Management Datastore Architecture of RFC 8342, so the data models do not have separate top-level or sibling containers for configuration data and operational state data.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD is a protocol that two ends of a path use to check that the path is still working, and to notice a failure quickly. It is used on its own and also by other protocols that need to know about failures. This RFC defines the data model a management system uses to configure it and to read its state, in the same way other YANG models are written.

sections.title: How the Model Is Split
sections.content:
Because BFD is used for liveness detection of various forwarding paths, there is no uniform key that identifies a BFD session, so the BFD data model is split into multiple YANG modules, each corresponding to one type of forwarding path. BFD for IP single-hop is in one module and BFD for MPLS in another. The main difference between the modules is how a BFD session is uniquely identified, that is, the key for the list that holds the sessions for that forwarding path. To avoid duplicating BFD definitions, the document defines common types and groupings that all the modules use.

A new control-plane protocol, bfdv1, is defined, and a bfd container is created under control-plane-protocol as specified in the YANG data model for routing management of RFC 8349. Four modules augment that container with their own information: ietf-bfd-ip-sh adds the ip-sh container for sessions over IP single-hop, ietf-bfd-ip-mh adds ip-mh for sessions over IP multihop, ietf-bfd-lag adds lag for sessions over a LAG, and ietf-bfd-mpls adds mpls for BFD over MPLS LSPs.

BFD can operate at the network device level, in logical network elements as described in RFC 8530, and in network instances as described in RFC 8529. At the device level the model is used as it is; in a logical network element or a network instance, the model augments the mounted routing model of that instance.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no single way to name a BFD session, because the session is identified by different things depending on the kind of path it runs over. So the model is split into four modules, one per kind of path, and they all add their part to the same BFD container in the routing configuration. The definitions they share, such as the timers, live in a common module so they are written once.

sections.title: The Configuration Model
sections.content:
The configuration model consists mainly of the parameters specified in BFD itself, for example the desired minimum transmit interval, the required minimum receive interval and the detection multiplier.

Some implementations keep the configuration of a BFD session under the client that uses it, for example under a routing application such as OSPF, IS-IS or BGP. Others centralise the configuration of BFD sessions under BFD itself, outside the several clients. The parameters of most interest to a client are those related to the multiplier and the intervals, because they affect how quickly the client converges after a failure. Other parameters, such as BFD authentication, are not specific to the client's requirements.

Configuration of BFD for all clients should be centralised, but that is a problem for clients that discover their peers automatically. An IGP does not have the peer address configured; the IGP is enabled on an interface and its peers are discovered, so an operator would first have to find the peer addresses, and configuration would have to be added every time a new peer appeared. To avoid this, the document defines a grouping called client-cfg-parms, which lets BFD clients configure BFD. An IGP can then hold the configuration for the sessions it needs: when a new peer is discovered the IGP creates a session to it, and when a peer goes away it removes the session. How the sessions are created and removed is outside the scope of the document, but it would typically use an API implemented by the BFD module. For clients that create sessions through their own configuration, the authentication parameters are still specified in BFD.

The basic configuration parameters are the detection time multiplier, the desired minimum transmit interval and the required minimum receive interval. Although BFD allows different values for the transmit and receive intervals, some implementations let the user specify one interval for both. The model supports that with a choice between min-interval, used for both, and desired-min-tx-interval with required-min-rx-interval, through the grouping base-cfg-parms that the modules for the various forwarding paths use.

For BFD authentication there is a key-chain reference, which points at the key chain model of RFC 8177, where the keys, the cryptographic algorithms and the key lifetime are all defined, and a meticulous flag that enables the meticulous mode of BFD.
sections.plainLanguage: The configuration holds the three numbers that decide how fast a failure is noticed: the multiplier, the interval at which packets are sent, and the interval at which packets are expected. A single interval can be set for both directions, or the two can be set separately. Authentication is configured by pointing at a key chain, which holds the keys themselves elsewhere, and by a flag that asks for the stricter mode of BFD.

sections.title: One Module for Each Kind of Path
sections.content:
For single-hop IP, the ip-sh node holds a list of sessions, each uniquely identified by the interface and the destination address pair, and uses the common configuration parameters. The node also holds a list of interfaces, used to specify the authentication parameters for sessions that BFD clients create. Since RFC 5880 and RFC 5881 do not say whether the Echo function operates continuously or on demand, the mechanism for starting and stopping it is implementation specific and is done by augmentation: either by configuration, which suits a continuous Echo function, or by an RPC, which suits an on-demand one.

For multihop IP, the ip-mh node holds session groups, because there can be several multihop sessions between a source and a destination when there are multiple paths. The key of a session group is the source address, belonging to the local system, and the destination address, belonging to the remote system. Two more parameters are provided: tx-ttl, the TTL of outgoing BFD control packets, and rx-ttl, the minimum TTL of incoming ones.

For MPLS label switched paths, the document addresses LSPs whose forwarding equivalence class is an IP address. The mpls node holds sessions uniquely identified by an IP prefix, and, again because there can be several paths, sets of them are grouped into session groups. These LSPs are unidirectional, so the egress node has no LSP configuration, and the BFD parameters for the egress node are added under mpls.

For link aggregation groups, configuring BFD on a LAG means having micro-BFD sessions on each member link. The BFD parameters are an attribute of the LAG, so they should sit under the LAG, but there is no LAG YANG data model to augment, so a lag node is added to the bfd node. The configuration is per LAG, with the destination IP address of the micro-BFD sessions given per LAG and per address family, for IPv4 and for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of path is named differently. A single-hop session is identified by the interface and the address at the far end. A multihop session group is identified by the two addresses, and it may contain several sessions when there is more than one path between them. An MPLS session is identified by the prefix of its forwarding equivalence class. A LAG session is identified by the name of the group and the address family, because BFD runs separately on each member link.

sections.title: The Operational State Model
sections.content:
The operational state model holds both the overall statistics for the BFD sessions running on the device and the per-session operational information. The overall statistics, such as the number of sessions and the number that are up, are available globally under the bfd node and also per type of forwarding path.

For each session, three categories of operational state data are shown. The first holds fundamental information about the session, such as the local discriminator, the remote discriminator and the ability to support Demand mode. The second holds the session-running information, for example the remote BFD state and the diagnostic code received, and the actual transmit interval between the control packets, which may differ from the configured desired minimum transmit interval, along with the actual receive interval and the actual transmit interval of the Echo packets. The third holds the detailed statistics for the session, for example when the session last moved up or down and how long it has been in that state.

For some path types there may be more than one session on the virtual path to the destination. With IP multihop and MPLS LSPs there can be several BFD sessions from the source to the same destination, to test the various equal-cost paths to it. This is represented by having multiple sessions under each session group.
sections.plainLanguage: The state model gives the totals first, then the detail of each session. For each session it reports what it is, how it is running now, and how it has been running: when the session last came up or went down and how long it has stayed that way. The intervals reported are the ones in use, which can differ from the ones that were configured.

sections.title: Notifications
sections.content:
The model defines notifications to tell end users about important events detected while the protocol runs. The local discriminator identifies the corresponding BFD session on the local system and the remote discriminator identifies the session on the remote system. The notifications also carry more important details about the sessions, for example the new state, the time in the previous state, the network instance, and the reason that the state changed. The notifications are defined for each type of forwarding path, and they use groupings for the common information.

The document defines no RPC operations.
sections.plainLanguage: When a session changes state, the model defines a notification to report it, with the reason for the change and how long the session was in its previous state. There are no remote procedure calls in this model, so nothing in it asks the device to do a one-off action.

sections.title: Example Configurations
sections.content:
The document gives four examples, written in XML. The first is a BFD IP single-hop session whose desired transmit interval and required receive interval are both 10 ms, keyed by the interface eth0 and the destination address 2001:db8:0:113::101, with both intervals set to 10000.

<bfd xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-bfd">
  <ip-sh xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-bfd-ip-sh">
    <sessions>
      <session>
        <interface>eth0</interface>
        <dest-addr>2001:db8:0:113::101</dest-addr>
        <desired-min-tx-interval>10000</desired-min-tx-interval>
        <required-min-rx-interval>10000</required-min-rx-interval>
      </session>
    </sessions>
  </ip-sh>
</bfd>

The second is a multihop session group with both intervals set to 150 ms and an rx-ttl of 240, between the source address 2001:db8:0:113::103 and the destination address 2001:db8:0:114::100.

The third is a LAG session on the interface Bundle-Ether1 of type ieee8023adLag, with the desired transmit and required receive intervals both set to 100000 and the IPv6 destination address 2001:db8:112::16.

The fourth is an MPLS session group for the forwarding equivalence class 2001:db8:114::/116, with both intervals set to 250 ms.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how a session is written in the XML form that a management system sends. A single-hop session names the interface and the address at the far end, a multihop session names the two addresses and a minimum TTL, a LAG session names the group and the address family, and an MPLS session names the prefix.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The YANG modules define a schema for data that is designed to be accessed through network management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport layer, where the mandatory secure transport is Secure Shell, and the lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS, where the mandatory secure transport is TLS.

The Network Configuration Access Control Model of RFC 8341 provides the means to restrict access for particular NETCONF or RESTCONF users to a preconfigured subset of the available operations and content.

A number of the data nodes are writable, and may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some environments. Write operations to them without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. The RFC lists the sensitive nodes: in the single-hop session list, the multiplier and the intervals affect the session, the source and destination addresses can be used to send BFD packets to unwitting recipients, and the key chain and meticulous nodes affect the security of the session; the same applies to the multihop session groups, the LAG sessions and the MPLS session groups. RFC 5880 describes how BFD mitigates the threat of sending packets to unwitting recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: The data is read and written over the management protocols, so the session must be protected in transit and access to it must be controlled by the usual access control model. Some of the writable values are worth guarding: the timers change how the sessions behave, and the addresses could be used to aim BFD packets at hosts that are not expecting them.
